status: Draft from the mishnah and Kehati (each item carries its mishnah number). Definitions are provisional until AnyDaf's master glossary covers them.

principles.t: Two people hold an object, each says it is his, and neither can prove it: each swears that he owns no less than half, and they split it. This applies whether they say 'I found it' or 'it's all mine'.

If one claims all and the other claims half, the claimant of all swears he owns no less than three quarters, the claimant of half swears no less than a quarter, and they divide three quarters to a quarter.
principles.note: Kehati (1:1): the claimant of half is conceding that the other half is his opponent's, so the dispute is only over the other half, which is divided; hence three quarters and a quarter.

principles.t: When neither side has witnesses, each swears. When both admit the other's claim, or there are witnesses, they divide without an oath.
One who found something must claim it at the time he takes hold of it, not after handing it to someone else.

Falling on a found object does not acquire (zakhah) it: whoever seizes it acquires it. A person's field can acquire an animal for him only if three conditions hold: others have not yet claimed it, the animal physically cannot leave the field, and the owner declares that his field acquires it.

What a person who is supported by him finds (minor children, Canaanite slave, wife) belongs to the supporter. What those independent of him find (adult children, a Hebrew slave, a divorced wife even before the ketubah is paid) is their own.

Found documents are returned or not according to whether we can be sure the owner lost them. A found loan document that records a lien (acharayut nekhasim) is not returned, since the court would collect from the property (the Sages say the same even without a lien; R. Meir disagrees, see below). Documents of giving (divorce, release of a slave, wills, gifts, receipts) are not returned, since the writer may have changed his mind and never given them.

Returned: documents drawn up by the court and the like, documents found in an identifiable bag, and a bundle (three documents tied together) whose names point to who lost it. A document of unknown nature among one's own documents waits until Elijah comes; torn documents are handled as their postscripts (simpon) say.

terms.def: The means of settling a claim when there are no witnesses.
To gain title to an object. In 1:3 by holding it and claiming it at that moment; in 1:4 also through one's field.

terms.term: my field acquires it for me
terms.def: A declaration by which a field's owner acquires an animal that is on his field and cannot leave it. It has no effect on an animal that can run or fly away.
Here, the divorce settlement that a husband owes his wife. Even before it is paid, what his divorced wife finds is hers.
A Canaanite (non-Jewish) slave is wholly owned, so what he finds belongs to his master. A Hebrew slave keeps what he finds.
A document that records a lien on the debtor's property: the court would collect repayment from the property.
A note attached to a document that states what must be done with it. The finder follows the postscript even if the document is torn or unreadable.
The document is left as it is: the finder must neither discard it nor give it to the creditor or the debtor.

debates.title: Is a found loan document without a lien returned to the lender?
debates.a: If it records no lien, he may return it, since the court would not collect from the property.
debates.b: In either case he does not return it, since in either case the court would collect from the property.

debates.title: Three documents found together: whose are they?
debates.a: Three documents in which one man borrowed from three others go back to the borrower; three in which one man lent to three go back to the lender. Kehati: if all three name the same man, he is the one who lost them.
debates.b: A bundle (three tied together) is returned.
